name: Hydra Fathom
geological_features: A global ocean broken by a single continental landmass at the south pole
Submarine plateaus at various depths creating distinct ecological zones
Hydrothermal vents along a mid-ocean ridge system
specific_features: A species of aquatic plant with multiple independent root systems that can regenerate the entire organism from any fragment
resources: Rare biological compounds from regenerative flora
Manganese and cobalt from ocean floor nodules
description: Hydra Fathom is a temperate ocean world with a single polar continent and an otherwise unbroken expanse of blue-green water. The ocean is layered in distinct zones defined by submarine plateaus that create shelves at various depths, each hosting its own community of photosynthetic and chemosynthetic organisms. The water is clear near the surface but darkens rapidly below the first plateau, the light filtered through dense floating mats of the planet's remarkable regenerative flora.

The atmosphere is mild and salt-tinged, the weather patterns dominated by oceanic cycles that bring reliable rains to the polar continent and long periods of calm to the mid-latitudes. The floating flora mats cover perhaps fifteen percent of the ocean surface, drifting with currents and growing at a rate that would be alarming if not for the grazers that keep them in check. The mats are thick enough to walk on in places, their surfaces a springy tangle of stems and photosynthetic bladders that support small invertebrate ecosystems.

The regenerative capacity of the dominant flora species has made it the subject of intense biological research. Any fragment, down to a few cells in size, can regrow into a complete organism with multiple independent root systems and reproductive structures. The mechanism involves a form of totipotency more extreme than anything observed in terrestrial biology, and the compounds responsible have attracted pharmaceutical interest for applications in human tissue regeneration. The species appears to be functionally immortal, with individual genetic lineages traceable back millions of years.

The polar continent serves as the primary base of operations for research teams, its solid ground a relief after weeks on the floating mats. The regenerative flora presents an unusual harvesting challenge, as every fragment that escapes collection grows into a new organism, making the species essentially inexhaustible but also impossible to contain. Control measures are in place to prevent accidental export, as the ecological consequences of introducing a functionally immortal, infinitely regenerative plant to a non-native environment are difficult to overstate.
